candidate.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: coordinate transitions of care, assess needs for referrals/resources, provide discharge planning and education, and collaborate with clients, caregivers, and the interdisciplinary team.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized stroke discharge and transition planning
candidate.educational_objective: Plan stroke discharge as an early, dynamic, individualized transition process that integrates rehabilitation/service needs, medications and secondary prevention, follow-up and safety/self-management planning, and caregiver education/readiness.

options.A: Use an individualized, evolving plan based on patient and family needs that addresses postacute rehabilitation and services, medication and secondary-prevention education, follow-up, safety and self-management needs, and caregiver readiness before transition.
options.B: Use the same discharge template for every stroke survivor because functional deficits, home environment, caregiver support, and rehabilitation needs do not change the transition plan.
options.C: Wait until the day of discharge to begin planning because early needs assessment does not affect selection of postacute services or caregiver preparation.
options.D: Focus only on the discharge date and medication list because rehabilitation placement, recurrent-stroke education, caregiver training, and follow-up are handled after the client leaves the hospital.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. A 2026 AHA scientific statement on nursing stroke care states that discharge planning should begin early, remain dynamic, and be guided by patient and family needs assessments; predischarge rehabilitation assessment is important for selecting the appropriate postacute setting and services. Current AHA nursing guidance also emphasizes education about lifestyle changes, medication adherence, recurrent-stroke symptom recognition, self-management and secondary prevention, and preparation of caregivers before discharge. B, C, and D fail to individualize the transition or defer essential planning until too late.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Stroke discharge planning should begin early, remain individualized and dynamic, incorporate rehabilitation/postacute service selection and secondary-prevention/self-management education, and prepare patients and caregivers for the transition rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all last-day process.
candidate.source_document_title: Targeted Nursing Interventions for Improving Stroke Care and Outcomes in the Rural Setting; Care of the Patient With Acute Ischemic Stroke (Posthyperacute and Prehospital Discharge)
candidate.source_locator: 2026 Targeted Nursing Interventions — Posthyperacute and Discharge: nurses educate about lifestyle changes, medication adherence, and early recurrent-stroke symptom recognition; discharge planning should begin early and remain dynamic based on patient/family needs; predischarge rehabilitation assessments help determine appropriate postacute setting and services. 2021 Posthyperacute/Predischarge statement and AHA commentary: discharge planning includes self-management, secondary stroke prevention, and caregiver education/readiness before discharge. 2026 AIS Guideline Section 5.7 supports multidisciplinary inpatient rehabilitation evaluation for appropriate postacute rehabilitation level.
candidate.source_version_date: Rural stroke nursing scientific statement published January 2026; posthyperacute/discharge scientific statement published 2021 and cited as associated guidance in the 2026 AIS guideline; accessed 2026-08-17
candidate.stem: A nurse begins discharge planning early for a client hospitalized with acute ischemic stroke. Which plan best reflects current stroke-care guidance?
